```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

These examples use `impact` to make excitation depend on observed event counts
or the current intensity components. Start with the
[state-dependent baseline examples](state-dependent-baseline.html) for simpler
state feedback. Each model below defines its own specification and simulated data.

See the [examples overview](extended_example.html) for other model topics.

```{r}
library(emhawkes)
```

## Hawkes flocking model

Here, $g$ denotes the additional excitation supplied by `impact`.
It depends on the observed state and need not depend on the mark.
In the Hawkes flocking model, the kernel components are
$$
\alpha = \begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} & 0 & 0 \\\alpha_{12}& \alpha_{11} & 0 & 0 \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{33} & \alpha_{34} \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{34} & \alpha_{33} \end{bmatrix},
$$
$$
g = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \alpha_{1w} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} \\
0 & 0 & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1w}1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} \\
\alpha_{2w} 1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2n}1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \\
\alpha_{2n} 1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2w}1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
$$

where

$$
C_1(t) = N_1(t) - N_2(t), \quad C_2(t) = N_3(t) - N_4(t).
$$
For details, see [Systemic risk in market microstructure of crude oil and gasoline futures prices: A Hawkes flocking model approach](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/fut.22048).

The `alpha` slot can contain a function that returns a matrix.
In the following example, the function returns a $4\times4$ matrix with some entries fixed at zero.
Only the parameters in `param` are estimated.
For simulation, a fixed matrix and a function returning the same matrix give the same model.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.02, 0.04, 0.04), nrow = 4)


alpha <- function(param = c(alpha11 = 0.2, alpha12 = 0.3, alpha33 = 0.3, alpha34 = 0.4)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha11"], param["alpha12"], 0, 0,
           param["alpha12"], param["alpha11"], 0, 0,
           0, 0, param["alpha33"], param["alpha34"],
           0, 0, param["alpha34"], param["alpha33"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}


beta <- matrix(c(rep(0.7, 8), rep(1.1, 8)), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

```

The `impact` function below implements the model definition.
Its `N` argument contains the counting process values, and `n` identifies the current event index.
Include both arguments because the function uses them, along with `...` to accept other arguments supplied by the package.
Use `N[n, "N1"]` to read one count directly, rather than extracting an entire column at every event.

```{r}
impact <- function(param = c(alpha1n=0.25, alpha1w=0.1, alpha2n=0.1, alpha2w=0.2),
                   N=N, n=n, ...){

  Psi <- matrix(c(0, 0, param['alpha1w'], param['alpha1n'],
                  0, 0, param['alpha1n'], param['alpha1w'],
                  param['alpha2w'], param['alpha2n'], 0, 0,
                  param['alpha2n'], param['alpha2w'], 0, 0), nrow=4, byrow=TRUE)

  ind <- N[n,"N1"] - N[n,"N2"] > N[n,"N3"] - N[n,"N4"]

  km <- matrix(c(!ind, !ind, !ind, !ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 !ind, !ind, !ind, !ind), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

  km * Psi
}

hspec_fl <- new("hspec",
                mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact = impact)
hspec_fl
```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
hr_fl <- hsim(hspec_fl, size=2000)
summary(hr_fl)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit_fl <- hfit(hspec_fl, hr_fl$inter_arrival, hr_fl$type)
summary(fit_fl)
```

This impact depends on observed event counts, so automatic selection uses the
C++ likelihood with numerical differentiation. No Jacobian is needed; R still
evaluates the impact.

```{r flocking-engine}
fit_diagnostics(fit_fl)$computation$engine
```

The same observed impact also supports automatic C++ intensity and residual replay.
No Jacobian is needed; retain the fit's initial-state arguments.

```{r flocking-replay}
replayed_fl <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = fitted_hspec(fit_fl),
  inter_arrival = hr_fl$inter_arrival, type = hr_fl$type, infer = TRUE),
  fit_initial_state(fit_fl)))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(fit_fl)), replayed = replayed_fl$loglikelihood)
```

## Bid-ask price model

This model describes bid and ask prices using a system of counting processes and their conditional intensities:

$$
N_t = \begin{bmatrix}
N_1(t) \\ N_2(t) \\ N_3(t) \\ N_4(t)
\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\lambda_t =
\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(t) \\ \lambda_2(t) \\ \lambda_3(t) \\ \lambda_4(t)
\end{bmatrix}
$$

In the unmarked case, the changes in ask and bid prices are $N_1(t) - N_2(t)$ and $N_3(t) - N_4(t)$, respectively.
The marked example below uses `Nc` to accumulate price changes.
The midprice $p(t)$ is the average of the ask and bid prices, including their initial levels.

The base intensity process is

$$\mu = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \mu_1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \ell(t) = \frac{L(t)}{p(t)} $$

where $L(t) \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ measures the bid-ask spread above its minimum level, so $L(t)=0$ corresponds to the minimum spread.
For details, see [Modeling bid and ask price dynamics with an extended Hawkes process and its empirical applications for high-frequency stock market data](https://academic.oup.com/jfec/article/21/4/1099/6513935?login=true).

In the `mu` function below, `n` identifies the current event index, and `Nc` is used to calculate the spread level and midprice.

```{r}
# presumed initial bid and ask prices
initial_ask_price <- 1250 #cents
initial_bid_price <- 1150 #cents

initial_level <- round((initial_ask_price - initial_bid_price) - 1)
initial_mid_price <- (initial_bid_price + initial_ask_price) / 2

mu <- function(param = c(mu1 = 0.08, zeta1 = 0.10), n=n, Nc=Nc, ...){

  if(n == 1){

    level <- initial_level
    mid <- initial_mid_price

  } else {

    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2])
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4])
    mid <- (ask + bid) / 2

  }

  if(level <= 0){
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], 0,
             0, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)
  } else {
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], param["zeta1"] * level / mid,
             param["zeta1"]*level / mid, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)

  }

}
```

In addition, the kernel is represented by

$$h(t, u) =
\begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{s1} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s2} & 0 \\   \alpha_{w1} & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{w2} \\  \alpha_{w2} & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{w1} \\  0 & \alpha_{s2} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s1} \\   \end{bmatrix},
$$

where

$$
\alpha_{n1}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{2j}(u) + \xi \ell(u), \quad \alpha_{n2}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{3j}(u) + \xi \ell(u),
$$

Here, $\xi \geq 0$ is a constant, and $\lambda_{ij}$ is a component of $\lambda_i$, defined by

$$\lambda_{ij}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^t h_{ij}(t, u) d N_j(u).$$

The following code places the constant part of $h$ in `alpha` and the state-dependent part in `impact`.
The `lambda_component_n` argument supplies the current pre-jump matrix of $\lambda_{ij}$ values.
This avoids allocating a full intensity history when only the current state is needed.
Individual components can be negative after a reset.
The equal decay rates used here allow simulation as long as the sum of the components in each row remains nonnegative.

```{r, warning=FALSE}

alpha <- function(param = c(alpha_s1=4, alpha_m=26, alpha_s2=5,
                            alpha_w1=11, alpha_w2=7)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha_s1"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s2"], 0,
           param["alpha_w1"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w2"],
           param["alpha_w2"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w1"],
           0, param["alpha_s2"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s1"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}

impact <- function(param = c(xi = 2.7), n=n, Nc=Nc, lambda_component_n = lambda_component_n, ... ){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
    # mid <- initial_mid_price
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2] - (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2])
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4])
    mid <- (ask + bid)/2
  }

  lambda_component_matrix <- lambda_component_n

  l2 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[2,]) # sum of second row
  l3 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[3,]) # sum of third row

  im <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0, 0,
                 0, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

}

beta <- matrix(rep(50, 16), nrow = 4, byrow=TRUE)

rmark <- function(n=n, Nc=Nc, type, ...){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
  }
  if (type[n] == 2 | type[n] == 3){
    min(level,  rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1)
  } else {
    rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1
  }
}


h_ba <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact=impact, rmark = rmark)
h_ba
```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
hr_ba <- hsim(h_ba, size=1000, lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4))
summary(hr_ba)
```

The following likelihood calculation and fit do not estimate the mark distribution because no `dmark` function is supplied.

```{r}
logLik(h_ba, inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type,
       mark = hr_ba$mark, Nc = hr_ba$Nc,
       lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4))
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mle_ba <- hfit(h_ba, inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type,
               mark = hr_ba$mark,
               lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4),
               final_hessian = "stable")
summary(mle_ba)
```

Automatic selection uses the C++ likelihood for this observed baseline and
sequential impact with numerical differentiation. The impact reads the current
state before its jump. No Jacobian is required. Inspect the saved engine record
to confirm which calculation was used and whether automatic selection fell back to R.

This example needs only the current component matrix, so it uses
`lambda_component_n`. Requesting `lambda_component` also stores the full history.
If a callback retains histories beyond its call, preserving those snapshots can
copy the history repeatedly. Cumulative allocation can then grow quadratically
with event count. This cost is
repeated for each likelihood evaluation during numerical optimization. Peak live
memory can be much smaller because old copies are reclaimed.

```{r bid-ask-engine}
fit_diagnostics(mle_ba)$computation$engine
```

Replay the fitted model with the same initialization and observations. Automatic
selection also uses C++ for its likelihood, intensity paths, and residuals.

```{r bid-ask-replay}
replayed_ba <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = fitted_hspec(mle_ba),
  inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type, mark = hr_ba$mark,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(mle_ba)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(replayed_ba$loglikelihood),
  as.numeric(mle_ba$maximum), tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

For the optional analytic fit, see the
[Bid-ask Jacobians and analytic gradient](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/computation.html#bid-ask-analytic-gradient).
That section continues from this example and gives the complete derivatives and fit.
Numerical differentiation remains the default.
